The uses of generative artificial intelligence in social research north and south: Comparing empirical evidence from surveys in Denmark and Mexico. Methodological Innovations. Type journal-article.
items.reason: **Yes, with a qualification.** There are now actual studies, not just AI-use counts, showing that researchers are unsure what is required of them and are asking for guidance. The strongest is Oxford University Press's September 2026 survey of 2,606 researchers: 74% agreed "there is a general lack of clarity about what AI use should be disclosed," and only about a third (36%) always keep a record of their AI use (OUP 2026, pp. 6, 27–28). Wiley's 2024 survey of 4,946 researchers found 63% named "a lack of clear guidelines and consensus on what uses of AI are accepted in their field and/or the need for more training" as a barrier, and 70% want publishers to say which uses are acceptable (Wiley 2025, pp. 4, 8). Both are publisher reports, not peer-reviewed. The peer-reviewed evidence points the same way but is smaller or narrower: medical corresponding authors (only 11.4% had institutional training; 69.7% wanted more; Ng et al. 2025), Danish researchers asking for "more support from their institutions" (Andersen et al. 2025), social researchers in Denmark and Mexico whose many "unable to answer" responses the authors read as "widespread uncertainty" (Schulz et al. 2026), and economists who could not agree on what AI use must be reported (Chemaya and Martin 2024). **The qualification:** every one of these measures uncertainty about *disclosure, acceptable use, or training*. None measures whether scholars know how to *verify or validate* an AI contribution. The closest verification evidence is about practice, not understanding: Desai, Card and Jacobs (2026, preprint) find validation of LLM measurements in flagship social-science journals "inconsistent and limited" and attribute it to "the limited guidance currently available." So the proposal can say scholars are asking for guidance and are unsure what to disclose. It should not say studies show scholars do not understand what verification requires. That is the gap the proposal fills, and it can be stated as a gap.

quotes.text: more support from their institutions

The authors interpret the high number of 'don't know' responses in the Mexican survey as evidence of hesitation and 'epistemic friction' regarding the use of generative AI, noting that informal conversations revealed uncertainty about the technology's inner workings.

items.reason: **The newest evidence shows the failure relocating, not resolving.** The first citation-claim alignment audit of ChatGPT-5 (thinking model, December 2025; 12 mental-health literature reviews; 333 citation-claims scored 1–4 against the full text of each cited source by two raters, kappa > 0.74) found that every one of the 209 cited publications existed — bibliographic fabrication effectively zero — yet only 43.5% of citation-claims were completely accurate; 19.8% were fabricated or contradicted by the cited source (including six direct contradictions of effect direction) and a further 18.3% contained major inaccuracies [Linardon et al. 2026, "Fluency Without Fidelity: Errors in Citation-Attributed Claims in Large Language Model-Generated Literature Reviews in Mental Health", Journal of Technology in Behavioral Science, 10.1007/s41347-026-00630-6, FULL-TEXT]. A real DOI at the end of a false sentence is exactly what the manuscript means by provenance without correspondence (our analysis).

items.reason: **1.2 Computational reproducibility is empirically terrible, and this is now measured, not asserted.** The distinctive feature of the last decade is that the field stopped arguing and started counting. Stodden, Seiler and Ma (2018) obtained artifacts for 44% of a *Science* sample and reproduced findings for 26%. Chang and Li (2022) reproduced 60 economics papers and titled the result "Often Not." Eubank (2016) found that of 24 papers under in-house replication review at *QJPS*, only four packages needed no modification and 14 produced results differing from the published paper. Trisovic et al. (2022) ran 9,000+ R files from Harvard Dataverse and found 74% failed to execute without error. This is the evidentiary base for any claim that a manuscript pipeline needs a gate.

quotes.text: Of the 24 empirical papers subject to in-house replication review between September 2012 and November 2015,1 only four packages did not require any modiﬁcations. Of the remaining 20 papers, 13 had code that would not execute without errors, eight failed to include code for results that appeared in the paper,2 and seven failed to include installation directions for software dependencies. Most troubling, however, was that 14 (58%) papers had results that diﬀered from those generated by the author’s own code.
